Having thus {hewn how the ancient Britfth language was in a manner extirpated by the Romans, Danes, and Saxons, and succeeded by the Saxon, and after that the Saxon blended with the Norman french, we {hall now mention two other cause sol change in the language : the first of these is owing to the Britons having -been a long time a trading nation, whereby offices, dignities, names of wares, and terms of traffic are introduced, which we take with the wares from the persons of whom we have them, and form them a new, according to the genius of our own tongue ; and besides this change in the language, arising from commerce, Britain’s having been a confiderable time fubjed to the fee of Rome, in ecclesiastical affairs, mull unavoidably introduce some Italian' words among us. Secondly, as to the particular properties of a lan guage, our tongue has undergone no smail mutation, or rather has received no smail improvement upon that account: for, as to the Greek and Latin, the learned have, together vith the arts and sciences now rendered familiar among us, introduced abundance; nay, almost all the terms of art in the mathematics, philofbphy, physic, and anatomy; and we have entertained many more from the Latin, French, fee. for the fake of neatness and elegancy : so that, at this day, our language, which about 1 800 years ago, was the an cient British, or Welch, fee. is now a mixture of Saxon, Teutonic, Dutch, Danish, Norman, and modern French, embellished with the Greek and Latin. Yet this, in our optnion, is so far from being a disadvantage to the Englifti tongue, as now spoke (for all languages have undergone changes, and do continually participate with each other) that it has so enriched it, as now to become the mod copious, significant, fluent, courteous, and masculine language in Europe, if not in the world

engrafting.c: ENGRAFTING, or Grafting, in gardening. See Gardening.

engrailed.c: ENGRAILED, or Ingrailed, in heraldry, a term derived from the French gres ly, hail ; and signifying a thing the hail has fallen upon and broke off the edges, leaving them ragged, or with half-rounds, or femicircks, (truck out of their edges.

engraving.c:
ENGRAVING, the art of cutting metals and precious stones, and representing thereon figures, letters, or whatever device, or design, the artist fancies;

Engraving, properly a branch of sculpture, is divided into feveral other branches, according to the matter whereon it is employed, and the manner of performing it.

The original way of engraving -on wood is denominated at present, with us, by cutting in wood ; that on metals with aquafortis, is named etching; that by the knife, burn flier, pix ich, and seraper, is called mezzotinto; that on Hones for tombs, fee. stone-cutting,; and that performed with the graver on metals or precious Hones, keeps alone the primitive name of engraving, being that which we (hall at present attend to.

Engraving on copper, is emplo. ed in representing portraits, ,histories, landskips, foliages, figures, buildings, he. either after paintings, or designs for that purpose.

It is performed with the graver on a plate of copper, which, being well polished, is covered over thinly with virgin-wax, and then smoothed, while warm, with a feather, so that the v/ax be of an equal thick-. nefs on the plate; and on this the draught or design, done in black lead, red cha!k, or sung summed ink, is laid with the face of the drawing on the wax: then they rub the backside, which will cause the whole design of the drawing to appear on the wax. The design, thus transferred, is traced through on the copper, with a point, or needle ; then heating the plate, and taking oft* the wax, the strokes remain to be followed, heightened, ire. according to the tenor of the design, with the graver, which must be very (harp and well pointed.

In the conduct of the graver consists almost all the art, which depends not so much upon rules as upon prad ice, the habitude, disposition, and genius of the artist, the principles of engraving being the same with those of painting; for if an engraver be not a perfect master of design, he can never hope to arrive at a degree of perfedion in this art. In conducing the strokes, or cuts, of the graver, he must observe the adion of the fingers, and of all their parts, with their outlines ; and remark how they advance towards, or fall back from his fight, and then condud his graver according to the risings or cavities of the muscles, or folds, widening the strokes in the light, and contra ding them in the (hades ; as also at the extremity of the outlines, to which he ought to condud die cuts of the graver, that the figures or objeds represented may not appear as if they gnawn ; and lightening his hand, that the outlines may be persedly found, without appearing cut or flit; and,- although his strokes. necessarily break off where a muscle begins, yet they ought always to have a certain connedion with each 0ther, so that the first stroke (should often serve to make the second, because this will (hew the freedom of the graver.

If hair be the fubjed, let the engraver begin his work by making the outlines of the principal locks, and (ketch them out in a careless manner, which may be finished, at leisure, with finer and thinner strokes to the very extremities.

The engraver must avoid making very acute angles, especially in representing fle(h, when he erodes the first strokes with the second, because it will form a very disagreeable piece of tabby like lattice-work, except in the reprefe.ntation of some clouds, in tempests, the waves of the sea, and in representations of (kins of hairy animals, and leaves of trees. So that the medium between Square and acute seems to be the best and most agreeable to the eye. He that would represent sculpture, must remember, that as statues, fee, are most commonly made of white marble, or stone, whose colour does not produce sach dark (hades as other matters do, they have no black to their eyes, nor hair of the fiead and beard flying in the air. If the engraver would

ENG ( 500 ) E N M

would preserve one quality and harmony in his works, he (should always (ketch out the principal objects of his piece before any part of them are fimffied.

The instruments necessary for this sort of engraving are, besides a graver, a cuff ion, or fand-bag, made of leather, to lay the plate on, in order to give it the necessary turns and motions ; a burnisher made of iron, or steel, round at one end, and usually flattish at the other, to rub out flips and failures, soften the strokes, &c. ; a scraper, to pare off the surface, on occasion ; and a rubber, of a black hat, or cloth rolled up, to fill up the strokes that they may appear the more visible.

In Engraving precious Jiones, they use either the diamond, or the emery. The diamond, which is the hardest of all stones, is only cut by itself, or with its own matter. The fir st thing to be done in this branch of engraving, is to cement two sough diamonds to the ends of two (ticks big enough to hold them steady in the hand, and to rub or grind them against each other till they be brought to the form desired. The dull or powder that is rubbed off ferves afterwards to polifii them, which is performed with a kind of mill that turns a wheel of soft iron. The diamond is fixed in a brass dissi, and, thus applied to the wheel, is covered with diamond dust, mixt up with oil of olives; and when the diamond is to be cut facet wife, they apply fir st one face, then another, to the wheel. Rubies, sapphires, and topazes, are cut and formed the same way on a copper wheel, and polished with tripoli diluted in water. Asto agate?, amethysts, emeralds, hyacinths, granates, rubies, and others of the fofter stones, they are cut on a leaden wheel, moistened with emery and water, and polished with tripoli, on a pewter wheel. Lapis-lazuli, opal, he. are -polished on a wooden wheel. To fashion and engrave vases of agate, crystal, lapis-lazuli, or the like, they make use of a kind of lathe, like that used by pewterers to hold the vessels, which are to be wrought with proper tools ; that of the engraver generally holds the tools, which are turned by a wheel ; and the vessel is held to them to be cut and engraved, either in relievo or otherwise; the tools being moistened, from time to time, with diamond dust and oil, or at least emery and water. To engrave figures or devices on any of these stones, when polished, such as medals, feals, he. they use a little iron wheel, the ends of whose axis are received within two pieces of iron, placed upright, as in the turner’s lathe ; and to be brought closer, or set further apart, at pleasure : at one end of the axis are fitted the proper tools, being kept tight by a ferret fr. Laftly, The wheel is turned by the foot, and the (tone applied by the hand to the tool, and is shifted and conducted as occasion requires.

The tools are generally of iron, ancl sometimes of brass ; their form is various, but it generally bears some resemblance to chissels, gouges, he. Some have small round heads, like buttons, others like ferrels, to take the pieces out, and others flat, he. when the stone has been engraven, it is polished on wheels of liajr-brufiies and tripoli.

Engraving on Jieel is chiefly employed in cutting feals, punchy, matrices, and dies proper for (hiking coins, medals, and counters. The method of engraving with the instruments, he. is the same for coins as for medals and counters : All the difference consists in their greater or lefs relievo, the relievo of coins being much' Id's confiderable than that of medals, and that of counters still lefs than that of coins.

Engravers in ftdel commonly begin with punches, which are in relievo, and serve for making the creux, or cavities, of the matrices and dies : though sometimes they begin with the creux, or hollowness, but then it is only when the intended work is to be cut very (hallow. The first thing done, is that of designing the figures ; the next is the moulding them in wax, of the size and depth they are to lie, and from this wax the punch is engraven. When the punch is finis lied, they give it a very high temper, that it may the better bear the blows of the hammer with which it is (truck to give the impression to the matrix.

The steel is made hot to soften it, that it may the more readily take the impression of the punch ; and after (Inking thp punch on it, in this state, they proceed to touch up or fini(h the strokes and lines, where by reason of their 'fineness or the too great relievo they are any thing tie festive, with steel gravers of different kinds, chissels, flatters, he. being the principal instruments used in graving on steel.

The figure being thus finiffied, they proceed to engrave the reft of the medal, as the mouldings of the border, the engrailed ring, letters, he., with little steel punches, well tempered, and very (harp.

ENGUICHE', in heraldry, is said of the great mouth of a hunting horn, when its rim is of a different colour from that of the horn itself.

engyscope.c: ENGYSCOPE, the same with microscope. See Microscope.

enharmonic.c: ENHARMONIC, in the ancient music, one of their genera or kinds of music, so called from its superior excellence ; though wherein it confided, fays Mr Malcom, is hard to say : it was allowed by all to be so very difficult, that few could ever pradife it.

enhydrus.c:
ENHYDRUS, in natural history, a genus of fiderochita or crustated ferrugineous bodies, formed in largo, and in great part empty cafes, inclosing a small quantity of an aqueous fluid.

Of this genus there are only two species : 1. The thick-ffielled enhydrus, 'with black, _ reddifti-brown, and yellow crusts. 2. The thinner (helled kind, with yellowi(h-brown and purple crusts; neither of which fer ments with aqua fortis, or gives fire with steel.

enixum.c:
ENIXUM, among chemists, a kind of neutral fait, generated of an acid and an alkali.

The fal enixum of Paracelsus, is the caput mortuum of spirits of nitre with oil of vitriol, or what remains in the retort after the distillation of this spirit ; being of a white colour, and pleasing acid taste.

ENMANCHE', in heraldry, is when lines are drawn from the centre of the upper edge of the chief to the fides, to about half the breadth of the chief; sign tying

ENT ( 5<

lying sleeved, or resembling a sleeve, from the French marc he.

enneagon.c: ENNEAGON, in geometry, a polygon with nine fides. See Polygon

enneahedria.c:
ENNE AHEDRIA, in natural history, a genus of columnar, cryftalliform, and double-pointed spars, composed of a trigonal column, terminated at each end by a trigonal pyramid.

Of this genus there are feveral species, distinguished by the length or shortness of the column and pyramids, none of which will give fire with (feel, but all of them ferment with, aqua fortis. See Sear.

enneandria.c: ENNEANDRIA, in botany. See Botany, p. 635. and Plate SUI. fig. 9.

ens.c:
ENS, among metapbyfiuans, denotes entity, being, or existence : this the schools call ens reali, and ens pofttivum, to distinguish it from their ens ratwnis, which is only an imaginary thing, or exists only in the imagination.

Ens, among chemists, imports the power, virtue, and efficacy which certain substances exert upon our bodies.

Ens, in geography, a cit^ of Germany, situated at the confluence of the Danube and the river Ens, about eighty miles south of Vienna : E. long. 140 20' , N. lat. 48° 1 6'.

enseeled.c: ENSEELED, in falconry, is said of a hawk that has a thread drawn through her upper eye-lid, and made fait under her beak, to take away the fight.

ensign.c:
ENSIGN, in the military art, a banner under which the soldiers are ranged according to the different companies or parties they belong to.

Ensign is also the officer that carries the colours, being the lowest commissioned officer in a company of foot, subordinate to the captain and lieutenant.

ensisheim.c: ENSISHEIM, a town of Germany, in the landgraviate of Alface, about fifty miles south of Strafburg: E. long. 70 30', N. lat. 470 jo'.

enskirken.c: ENSKIRKEN, a town of Germany, fifteen miles southwest of Cologn.

entablature.c: ENTABLATURE, or Entablement, in architecture, is that part of an order -of a column which is over the capital, and comprehends the architrave, frieze, and corniche. See Architecture.

entabler.c:
ENTABLER, in the menage, the fault of a horse whose cro supe goes before his shoulders in working upon volts ; which may be prevented by taking hold of the right rein, keeping your right leg near, and removing your left leg as far from the horse’s shoulder as possible.

This is always accompanied with another fault called ac user. See Acuser.

ENTAIL. See Tailzie.

ENTE', in heraldry, a method of marshalling. more frequent abroad than with us, and signifying g afted or ingrafted.

We have, indeed, one instance of ante in the fourth grand quarter of his majesty’s royal ensign, whose blazon is Brunswick and Lunenburg impaled With ancient Saxony, ante en pain se, grafted in point.

entelechia.c:
ENTELECHIA, a word used by Aristotle to express Vol. II. No. 47.

)i ) ENT

the soul, and which, not occurring in ar.y other author, has given the commentators upon that pliilofopher great trouble to discover its true meaning.

enterocele.c: ENTEROCELE, in surgery, a tumor formed by a prolapsion of the intestines through the rings of the abdomen, and processes of the peritonaeum, into the scrotum. See Surgery. "

enterology.c: ENTEROLOGY, a term used by physicians, for a d-'scourse or treatise on the contents of the head, breast, and abdomen.

enteromphalus.c: ENTEROMPH ALUS, the same with a hernia umbilicalis, or rupture at the navel.

entersole.c: ENTERSOLE, in architecture, a kind of little story, sometimes called a mezanzme, contrived, occasionally at the top of the first story, for the conveniency of a wardrobe isc.

enthusiasm.c:
ENTHUSIASM, a transport of the mind, whereby it is led to think and imagine things in a sublime, surprising, yet probable manner. This is the enthusiasm felt in poetry, oratory, music, painting, sculpture, <fac.

Enthusiasm, in a religious sense, implies a transport of the mind, whereby it fancies itself inspired with some revelation, impulse, &c. from heaven..

enthusiast.c: ENTHUSIAST, a person possessed with enthusiasm. See the preceding article.

enthymeme.c:
ENTHYMEME, among logicians, denotes a syllogism, perfect in the mind, but imperfect in the expression, by reason one of the propositions is suppressed, as being easily supplied by the underftandmg of those with whom we discourse.

ENTOMON, in zoology. See Oniscus.

entrepas.c:
ENTREPAS, m the manege, a broken pace or going, that is neither walk nor trot, but has somewhat of an amble.

This is a pace or gait of such horses as have no reins or back, and go upon their shoulders ; or, of such as are spoiled in their limbs.

Entering-ladders, in a ship, are of two forts; one used by the vest ers fides, in a harbour, or in fair weather, for persons to go in and out of the ship : the other is made of ropes, with small ftavts for steps ; and is hung out of the gallery to enter into the boat, or to come aboard the ship, when the sea runs so high that they dare not bring the boat to the ship’s side for fear of staving it.

enirochus.c:
ENI ROCHUS, in natural history. See Isis.

ENTRY of an heir , in Scots law, that form of law by which an heir veils in himself a proper title to his predecessor’s estate. See Precept of Clare Constat.

Bill of ENTRY, in commerce. See BiLl.

In making entries inwards, it is usual for merchants to include all the goods they have on board the same Ihip in one bill, though sometimes they may happen to be upwards of twenty feveral kinds ; and in cafe the goods are sliort entered, additional or post entries are now allowed ; though formerly the goods, so entered "Were forfeited. As to bills of entry outwards, or including goods to be exported, upon delivering them, and paying the customs, you will receive a small piece

E p a ( :

of parchment called a cocket, which testifies your payment thereof, and all duties for such goods.

If feveral forts of goods are exported at once, of which some aTe free, and others pay customs ; the exporter mud have two cockets, arid therefore mull make two entries ; one for the goods that pay, and the other for the goods that do not pay custom.

Entries of goods, on which a drawback is allowed, mull likewise contain the name of the Ihip in which the goods were imported, the importer’s name, and time of entry inwards. The entry being thus made, and an oath taken that the customs for those .goods were paid as the law directs, you must carry it to the collector and comptroller, or their deputies ; who, after examining their books, will grant warrant, which must be given to the surveyor, Earcher, or landWaiter, for them to certify the quantity of goods; after which the certificate must be brought back to the collector and comptroller, or their deputies, and oath made that the said goods are really Ihipped, and not landed again in any part of Great Britain.

envelope.c:
ENVELOPE, in fortification, a work of earth, sometimes in form of a simple parapet, and at others like a small rampart with a parapet: it is raised sometimes on the ditch, and sometimes beyond it.

ENVIRONNE', in heraldry, signifies surrounded with other things : thus, they say, a lion environnri with so many bezants. See Bezant. -

enumeration.c: ENUMERATION, an account of feveral things, in which mention is made of every particular article.

envoy.c: ENVOY, a perfoo deputed to negociate some affair with any foreign prince or state. Those sent from the courts of France, Britain, Spain, <bc to any petty prince or Hate, such as the princes of Germany, the republics of Venice, Genoa, <bc. go in quality of envoys, pot embassadors ; and such a character only do those persons bear, who go from any of the principal courts of Europe to another, when the affair they go upon is not very solemn or important. There are envoys ordinary and extraordinary, as well as embassadors ; they are equally the same under the protection of the Jaw of nations, and enjoy all the privileges of embassadors, only differing from them in this, that the same ceremonies are not performed to them.

envy.c: ENVY, in ethics, an un easiness of the mind, caufed by the consideration of a good we defire, obtained by one we think lefs worthy of it than ourselves. See Passion, and Morals.

epact.c: EPACT. See Astronomy, Of the Dlvijion of Time.

epanorthosis.c:
EPANORTHOSIS, in rhetoric, a figure by which a person corrects, or ingeniously revokes, what he just before alledged, as being too weakly expressed, in order to add something stronger, and more conformable to the passion with which he is agitated.

The epanorthosis is distinguished into two kinds. The one is-when we correCt Or revoke" the word, as-in ; tlpe following example of the apostle, But I laboured more abundantly than they all : yet not 1, but the grace of God, 'which 'was with me, I Cor. xv. io. . where, what, he first attributed to his own merit, he tchufes afterwards to call .the work of grace, 3$ beinj*

;oi ) E P H

the principal cause. The second kind of epanorthosis, is when we correCt or revoke the sentiment, as in the following of Cicero: Italiamornare, quam donmm fum, nat suit : qiiamquani, Italia ornata , domus ipsa mi hi videtur or n at tor.

eparer.c: EPARER, in the menage, signifies the flinging of a horse, or his yerking and striking with his hind-legs.

epaulement.c: EPAULEMENT, in fortification, a work raised to cover sidewise, is either of earth, gabions, or fascines loaded with earth. The epaulements of the. places of arms for the cavalry,, at the entrance of the trenches, are generally of fascines mixed with earth.

epenthesis.c:
EPENTHESIS, in grammar, the interposition or infertion of a letter or syllable in the middle of a word; as alituum , for alitum ; relligio, for religio ; indupe - rator, for imperater, &c,

EPERLANUS, in ichthyology. See Salmo.

epha.c:
EPHA, orEpHAH, in Jewish antiquity, a measure for things dry, con tang 1.0961 of a but lies.

EPH/ETUM, in botany. See Ranunculus.

ephedra.c: EPHEDRA, the sea-grape, or shrub horse tail, in botany, a genus of the dioecia monadelphia class. The cahx of the amentum of the male and female is divided into segments ; the corolla is wanting in bath ; the (lamina are seven ; there are two pistils, and two feeds covered with a kind of cup berry. There are two species, none of them natives of Britain.

ephemery.c: EPHEMERY, in medicine, the name of a species of fever continuing the space of one day, or sometimes more ; for the medical writers express themselves by ephemera Jimplex, vel plurima dierum. See Medicine.

ephemera.c: EPHEMERA, the day fly, in zoology, a genus belonging to the order of neuroptera. It has no teeth or palp*; there are two large protuberances above the eyes; the wings are erect, the two hind ones being, largest ; and the tail is bristly. There are eleven species, distinguished by their colour and the number of bridles in their tail. This fly derives its name from the circumstance of its living but one day.

ephemerides.c:
EPHEMERIDES, in literary history, an appellation given to those books or journals, which (hew the motions and places of the .planets for every day of the year.

• It is from, the tables contained in these ephemerides-, that eclipses, and all the variety of aspe&s of the planets, are found.

ephialtes.c: EPHIALTES, in medicine, the same with the incubus, or night-mare See Incubus.

ephod.c:
EPHOD, in Jewish antiquity, one part of the priestly habit; being a kind of girdle, which, brought from behind the neck over the two (boulders, and hanging down before, was put cross the stomach, then carried round the waift, and made use of as a girdle to the tunic

There were two forts of ephods, one of plain linen for the priests, and the other embroidered for the high prie il.

ephori.c:
EPHORI, in Grecian antiquity, magistrates established

E P I ( 503 ) E P 1

in ancient Sparta to balance the regal power. The authority of the ephori was very great. They seine times expelled and even put to death the kings, and abolished or suspended the power of the other magi- (trates, calling them to account at pleasure. There were five of them, others say nine. They presided ia the public (shews and festivals. They were entrusted with the public treasure, made war and peace, and were so absolute, that Aristotle makes their government equal to the prerogative of a monarchy. They were e^ahlilhed by Lycurgus.

EPHYDRUM in botany. See Equisetum.

EPIC, or Heroic poem. *See Compos tion.

epicedium.c: EPICEDIUM, in ancient poetry, a poem rehearsed during the funeral solemnity of persons of diftinXion.

epicoene.c:
EPICOENE, in grammar, a term applied to nouns, which, under the same gender and termination, mark indifferently the male and female species.

EPICUREAN philosophy, the cox rine or system of philosophy maintained by Epicurus and his followers.

His philosophy confided of three parts, canonical, physical. and etherial. The first was about the canons, or rules of judging. The censure which Tully passes upon him for his despising logic, will hold true only with regard to the logic of the Itoics, which he could not approve of, as being too full of nicety and quirk. Epicurus was not acquainted with the analytical method of division and argumentation, nor was he so curious in modes and formation as the (stoics. Soundness and simplicity of sense, af sided with some natural reflexions, was all his art. . His search after truth proceeded only by the senses, to the evidence of which he gave so great a certainty, that he confidered them as an infallible rule of truth, and termed them the first natural light of mankind.

In the second part of this philosophy he laid down atoms, space, and gravity, as the first principles of all things : he did not deny the exist ence of God, but thought it beneath his maja dy to concern himself with human affairs: he held him a blessed immortal being, having no affairs of his own'to take care of, and above meddling with those of others.

As to his ethics, he made the supreme good of man to consid in pleasure and consequently supreme evil in pain. Nature itself, fays he, teaches us this truth, and prompts us from our birth to procure whatever gives us pleasure, and avoid what gives us pain. To this end he proposes a remedy against the Iharpnefs of pain : this was to divert the mind from it, by turning our whole attention upon the pleasures we have formerly enjoyed : he held that the wife man mud be happy, as long as he is wife •, that pain, not depriving him of his wisdom, cannot step tive him of his happiness.

There is nothing that has -a fairer (hew of honesty than the moral cox rine of Epicurus. Gaffendus pretends, that the pleasure in which this philosopher has fixed the sovereign good, was nothing elfe but the highed tranquillity of mind in conjunXioD with the trod pet sect health of body : but Tully, Horace, and

Plutarch, as well as almost all the fathers of die church, give us a very different reprefentatiofl : indeed the nature of this pleasure, in which the chief happiness is (supposed to> be feated, is a grand problem in the niorals of Epicurus. Hence there were two kinds of Epicureans, the rigid and the remiss : the first were thole who under stood Epicurus’s notion of pleasure in. the bed sense, and placed all their happiness in the pure pleasures of the mind, resulting from the.praXice of virtue: the loose or remiss Epicureans, taking, the words of that philosopher in a gross sense, placed all their hap nefs in bodily pleasures or debauchery. EPICYCLE, in the ancient adorn omy, a little circle whose centre is in the.circumference Of a greater circle* or it is a small orb, or sphere, which being fixed in. the deferent of a planet, is carried along with it ; and yet, by its own peculiar motion, carries the planet fad- * ened to it round us proper centre.

It was by means of epicyales, that Ptolemy and his followers solved the various phenomena of the planets*- but more especially their Itations and retrogradations. EPICYCLOID, in geometry, a curve generated by the revolution of the periphery of a circle, along the convex or concave side of the periphery of another cirde. EPICYEMA, among physicians, denotes a superfoetation ; being a false conception or mole happening after the birth of a regular foetus.

epidemia.c: EPIDEMIA, in Grecian antiquity, ftdivals kept in honour of Apollo and Diana, at the dated seasons when these deities, who could not be present every where, were supposed to visit different places, in order to re-' cciya the vows of their adorers EPIDEMIC, among physicians, an epithet of diseases which at certain times are popular ; attacking great numbers at or near the same time. See Medicine. EPIDENDRUM, in botany, a genus of the gynandria diandria class. The neXarium is oblique, reflected, and Ihaped likea turban. There are thirty species,' none of them natives of Britain.

epidermis.c: EPIDERMIS, in anatomy. See Anatomy, p. 2tc EPIDIDYMIS, in anatomy. See Anatomy, p. ijj, EPIGASTRIC region, a part or subdivision of thei abdomen. See Anatomy, p. 256-.

epiglottis.c: EPIGLOTTIS, in anatomy, one of the cartilages of the larynx, or wind-pipe. See Anatomy, p. 281. EPIGR AM, in poetry, a (short poem in verse, treating, only of one thing, and ending. with some lively, ingenious, and natural thought or point.

epigraphe.c: EPIGRAPHE, among antiquarians, denotes the in-- scription of a building, pointing out the time when, the persons by whom, the ufes, and the like, for which it was ereXed.

epilepsy.c:
EPILEPSY, in medicine, the same with what is otherwise called the falling sickness, from the patient’s falling sudden) y to the ground. See Medicine. EPILOBIUM, in botany, the willow herb, a genus of the oXandria monogynia class. The calix is divided into fourfegmems, and the corolla confi/is of fourpetals', the capsule is oblong, and below the flower* and the feeds are pappous. There are seven spe> ies • all of them natives of Britain, viz. the anguflifolium’ or rose bay

E P I ( 504

rosebay willow-herb ; the hirfutum, or small-flowered hairy billow herb; the ramofum, great flowered willow-herb, or codlings and cream; the montanum, or smooth-leaved willow herb ; the tetragonum, or narrow-leaved willow-herb ; the palus tre, or marfli willow herb ; and the alpinum, or mountain willow-herb.

epilogue.c:
EPILOGUE, in oratory, the end or conclusion of a discourse, ordinarily containing a recapitulation of the principal 'matters delivered.

Epilogue, in dramatic poetry, a speech addressed to the audience after the play is over, by one of the principal astors therein, usually containing some reflexions on certain incidents in the play, especially those in the part of the person that speaks it.

epimedium.c: EPIMEDIUM, barren wort, in botany, a genus of the tetrandia monogynia class. It has four cap-snap ed neCtaria lying upon the petals ; the corolla cpnlifts of four petals ; and the calix is caducous. 1 here is but one species, a native, of Germany ^

epiphany.c: EPIPHANY, a Christian festival, otherwise called the Manifestation of Christ to the Gentiles, observed on the sixth of January, in honour of the appearance of our Saviour to the three magi, or wife-men, who came to adore him and bring hinvprefents. The feast of epiphany was not originally a distinct festival, but made a part of that of the nativity of Christ, which being celebrated twelve days, the first and last of which were high or chief days of solemnity, either of these might properly be called epiphany, as that word signifies the appearance of Christ in the world.

epiphonema.c: EPIPHONEMA, in rhetoric, a sententious exclamation containing a lively remark placed at the end of a discourse or narration.

epiphora.c: EPIPHORA, in medicine, a preternatural defluxion of the eyes, when they continually discharge a (harp ferous humour, which excoriates the cheeks. See Medicine.

epiphysis.c: EPIPHYSIS, in anatomy. See Anatomy, Part I.

epiplocele.c: EPIPLOCELE, in medicine, is a kind of hernia, or rupture, in which the omentum subsides into the scrotum.

epiploomphalon.c:
EPIPLOOMPHALON, in medicine, an hernia umbilicalis, proceeding from the omentum falling into the region of the umbilicus or navel.

EPIPLOON. See Omentum.

episcopacy.c: EPISCOPACY, the quality of episcopal government, or that form of chuixh-dtfcipline, wherein diocefian bishops are established dift'nX from and superior to priests or presbyters. See Bishop

episcopalians.c:
EPISCOPALIANS, in church history, an appellation given, to those who prefer the episcopal government and disc pl’ne to all others..

By the test aft, none but episcopalians, or members of the church of England, are qualified to enjoy any office civil or military.

EPISCOPUS. See Bishop.

episode.c:
EPISODE, in poetry, a separate incident, story, or action, which a poet invents, and connects with his principal .ad tied, that his work may abound with a greater diver-

) E P I

sity of events ; though, in a more limited sense, all the particular incidents whereof the afhon or narration is compounded, are called episodes. See Composition.

epispastic.c:
EPISPASTIC, in medicine, a topical remedy, which being applied to the external parts of the body, at-

. trasss the humours to that part.

EPIS1 ATES, in the Athenian government, was the prefident of the proedri. See Proedri,

epistemonarch.c: EPISTEMONARCH, in the ancient Greek church, an officer of great dignity, who had the care of every thing relating to faith, in the quality of censor. His office answered pretty nearly to that of master of the sacred palace at Rome.

episile.c: EPISILE, denotes the same with a missive letter; but is now chiefly used in speaking of ancient writings, as the epistles of St Paul, epistles of Cicero, epiities of Pliny ,6c.

epistolary.c: EPISTOLARY, something belonging to an epistle. See Epistle.

epistrophe.c: EPISTROPHE, in rhetoric, a figure, wherein that which is supposed of one thirvj, is ttrongly affirmed of another: thus, Are they^Hebrenus ? so am /. Are they Jf ratlins ? so am 1. Are they oj the feed of Abraham? so am /, &c,

epistyle.c: EPISTYLE, in the ancient architecture, a term used by the Greeks for what we call architrave, viz. a massive piece of stone or 'wood, laid immediately over the capital of a column.

epitaph.c: EPITAPH, a monumental inscription in honour or memory of a person defunct, or an inscription engraven or cut on a tomb, to mark the time of a person’s decease, his name, family ; and, usually, some eulogium of his virtues, or good qualities.

epitasis.c:
EPITASIS, in ancient poetry, the second part or division of a dramatic poem, wherein the plot, entered upon in the first part, or protasis, was carried on, heightened; and worked up, till it arrived at hs state, or • height, called catastasis.

Epitasis, in medicine, the increase of a dfeafe, or beginning of a paroxysm, particularly in a -fever.

epithalamium.c:
EPITHALAMIUM, in poetry, a nuptial song, or composition, in praise of the bride and bridegroom, praying for their prosperity, for a happy offspring,

Among the Greeks, the married couple weienofooner bedded, than the young men and maids gathered round the door, dancing and singing the epithalamium, shouting and stamp leg with their feet, with intention to drown the maid’s cries.

epithem.c: EPITHEM, in pharmacy, a kind of fomentation, or remedy of a spirituous or aromatic kind, applied externally to the regions of the heart, liver, &c. to (Lengthen and comfort the same, or to correct some intemperature thereof. See Fomentation.

epithet.c:
EPITHET, in poetry and rhetoric, an adjeAive express ir.g some quality of a substantive to which it is joined ; or such an adjedive as is annexed to substantives by way of ornament and illustration, not to make up an essential pan of the description. Nothing, fays Aristotle, tires the reader more than too great a redundancy of epithets, or epithets placed improperly; and yet nothing

E U ( 505

nothing la so e fieri tial in poetry as a proper life of them. The writings of the befl poets are full of them, especially Virgil.

TPiTOME, in literary history. See Abridgement.

epitritus.c: EPITRITUS, in prosody, a foot confiding of three long syllables and one short.

epizeuxis.c: EPIZEUXIS, in rhetoric, a figure which repeats the same word, without any other intervening; such is that of Virgil, Nunc ,■ nunc, infurgite remit.

epocha.c: EPOCHA, in chronology, a term or fixed point of time, whence the succeeding years are numbered or accounted. . See Astronomy, p.487.

epode.c:
EPODE, in lyric poetry, the third or lad part of the ode; the ancient ode being divided into strophe, antistrophe, and epode. See Ode.

EPOPOEIA.in poetry, the dory, fable, or fubjed treated of in an epic poem.

epotides.c: EPOTIDES, in the naval archil endure of the ancients, two thick blocks of u'ood, one on each side the prow of a galley, for warding off the blows of the rodra of the enemy’s vefftls.

eppingen.c: EPPINGEN, a town of Germany, situated about ten miles north of Halibron.

epsom.c: EPSOM, a town of Surty, about fifteen miles south-well of London ; much resorted to on account of 'its medicinal waters ; from which the bitter purging fait being first extra ded, got the name of Epsom-salt. At pre sent, however, the bitter purging fait is procured from the bittern, remaining after the crystallization of common fait ; and this is found to answer all the purposes of that first obtained from Epsom-waters, and goes by its name. See Chemistry.

epulones.c: EPULONES, in Roman antiquity, ministers who assisted at the sacrifices, and had the care of the sacred banquet committed to them.

equable.c: EQUABLE, an appellation given to such motions as always continue the same in degree of velocity, without being either accelerated or retarded. See Mechanics.

equal.c:
EQUAL, a term of relation between two or more things oF the same magnitude, quantity, or quality.

Mathematicians speak of equal lines, angles, figures, circles, ratios, solids.

equality.c: EQUALITY, that agreement between two or more things, whereby they are denominated equal.

equanimity.c: EQUANIMITY, in ethics, denotes that even and calm frame of mind and temper, under good or bad fortune, whereby a man appears to be neither puffed up nor overjoyed with prosperity, nor dispirited, foured, or rendered uneasy by adversity.

equation.c:
EQUATION, in algebra. See Algebra, p. 100.

Equation of time, in astronomy and chronology, the redudion of the apparent time or motion of the sun, to equable, mean, or true time. See Astronomy, p. 459.

equator.c: EQUATOR, in geography, a great circle of the terrestrial globe, equid-'stant from its poles, and dividing it .into two equal hemispheres ; one north, and the other south. See Geography.

equerry.c:
EQUERRY, jn the British customs, an officer of (late, under the master of the horse.

Vol. II. No. 47. 4

) E e^tr

There are five equerries, who ride abroad with his majesty : for which purpose they give their attendance monthly, one at a time and are allowed a table.

As to the equerries of the crown stable, they have this diftind appellation, as being employed in mounting, managing, and breaking the faddle horses for his majesty’s use, and holding his stirrup.

EQUES auratus, isufedfora knight hatchel or, called euratus , q. d. gilt, because anciently none but knights were allowed to beautify their armour, or 0ther habiliments for war, with gold.

EQUESTRIAN statue, signifies the statue of a person mounted on horseback.

Equestrian order, among the Romans, signified their knights, or equites ; as also their troopers, or horsemen in the field ; the first of which orders flood in con.- tradiftindion to the senators, as the last did to the foot, military, or infantry: each of these diftindions was introduced into the (late by Romulus.

equiangular.c:
EQUIANGULAR, in geometry, an epithet given to figures, whose angles are all equal : such are a square, an equilateral triangle, <bc.

EQUICRURAL, in geometry. See Isosceles.

equidistant.c: EQUIDISTANT, an appellation given to things placed at equal distance from same fixed point, or place, to which they are referred.

equilateral.c: EQUILATERAL, in general, something that hath equal fides, as an equilateral angle.

equilibrium.c: EQUILIBRIUM, in mechanics, is when the two ends of a lever or balance hang so exadly even and level, that neither doth ascend or descend, but keep in a position parallel to the horizon ; which is occasioned by their being both charged with an equal weight.

equimultiples.c:
EQUIMULTIPLES, in arithmetic and geometry, are numbers or quantities multiplied by one and the same number or quantity. Hence, equimultiples are always in the same ratio to each other, as the Ample quantities before multiplication : thus, if 6 and 8 are multiplied by 4, the equimultiples 24 and 32 will be toeach other as 6 to 8.

-EQUINOCTIAL, in astronomy, a great circle of the celestial globe, whose poles are the polesof the world. See Astronomy, and Geography.

equinox.c:
EQUINOX, the time when the sun enters either of the equine dial points, where the ecliptic interfeds the equine dial. See Astronomy.

Precefion of the EqyiNoX.ES. See Astronomy.

equisetum.c: EQUISETUM, or horse-tail, in botany, a genus of the cryptogamia filices class. The frudification is disposed on an oblong spike, and of an orbicular figure. There are seven species, six of which are natives of Britain, viz. the sylvaticum, or wood horse-tail; the ar verse, or corn horse-tail; the palus tre, or marsh horse-tail; the fluviatile, or river horse-tail; the limofum, or smooth horse-tail; and the hyemale, or rough horse-taiL

equity.c: EQUITY, in a general sense, the virtue of treating all other men according to common reason and justice, or as we would be gladly treated ourselves, when we understand aright what is our due. See Justice. .

equivalent.c:
EQUIVALENT, an appellation given to things which 5 L agree

E U ( 506

agree in nature, or other circumstances, as force, vir equivocal terms or words, among logicians, are those which have a doubtful or double meaning.

According to Mr Locke, the doubtfulness and uncertainty of words has its cause more in the ideas themselves, than in any incapacity of the words to signify them ; and might be avoided, would people always use the same term to denote the same idea, or collection of ideas : but, adds he, it is hard to find a discourse on any subject where this is the cafe ; a practice which can only be imputed to folly, or great dishonesty ; since a man, in making up his accounts, might with as much fairness use the numeral characters sometimes for one, sometimes for another collection of unities.

Equivocal generation, the production of animals, without the intercourse between the fexes, by the influence of the sun or stars, foe.

EQUULEUS, or Ecuuleus, in antiquity, a kind of rack u fed for extorting a confession, at first chiefly practised.on slaves, but afterwards made use of against the Christians.

The equuleus was made of wood, having holes, at certain distances, with a screw, by vhich the criminal was f retched to the third, sometimes to the fourth, or fifth holes, his arms and legs being fattened on the equus cas with cords ; and thus was hoitted aloft, and extended in such a manner, that all his bones were dislocated. In this state red-hot plates were applied to his body, and he was goaded in the fides with an instrument called ungula.

Equuuus, in astronomy. See Astronomy, p. 487.

EQUUS, the Horse, in zoology, a genus of quadrupeds belonging to the order of belluae. This genus comprehends the horse, the ass, and the zebra ; they have six erect and parallel fore-teeth in the upper jaw, and six fotnewhat prominent ones in the under jaw ; the dog-teeth are limitary, and at a confiderable distance from the reft ; and the feet con fill of an undivided hoof. The hprfe is a domestic animal, and the figure and dimensions of his body are so well known, that a general description is altogether unnecessary. We shall therefore confine ourselves to the natural history of this noble animal.

The horse, in a domestic state, is a bold and fiery animal ; equally intrepid as his matter; he faces danger " and death with ardour and magnanimity. He delights in the noise and tumult of arms, and feenxs to feel the glory of vidlory,: he exults in the chafe; his eyes fpatkle with emulation in the course. But though bold and intrepid, he is docile and tradable : he knows how to govern and check the natural vivacity and fire of his temper. He not only yields to the’ hand, but seems to consult the inclination of his rider. Constantly obedient to the impressions he receives, his motions are entirely regulated by the will of his master. He in some measure resigns his very existence to the pleasure of man. He delivers up his whole powers ; he reserves

) E (^ u

nothing ; he will rather die than disobey. Who could endure to see a character so noble abused ! Who could be guilty of such gross barbarity !

This character, though natural to the animal, is in some measure the effect of education, His education commences with the loss of liberty, and it is finished by constraint. The slavery of the horse is so ancient and so universal, that he is but rarely seen in a natural state. Several ancient writers talk of wild horses, and even mention the places where they were to be found. Herodotus takes notice of white savage horses in Scythia ; Aristotle fays, they are to be found in Syria ; Pliny, in the northern regions ; and Strabo, in Spain and the Alps. Among the moderns, Leardon say«, that wild horses are to be found in the Highlands of Scotland, and the Orkney Ides ; Olaus, in Muffcovy ; Dapper, in the island of Cyprus ; Leo and Marmol, in Arabia and Africa, foe. But, as Europe is almost equally inhabited, wild horses are not to be met with in any part of it; and those of America -were originally transported from Europe by the Spaniards ; for this species of animals did not exit in the new world. The Spaniards carried over a great number of horses, left them in different islands, foe., with a view to propagate that useful animal in their colonies. These have multiplied incredibly in the vast desarts of those thinly peo-* pled countries, where they roam at large, without any restraint. M. de Salle relates, that he saw, in the year 1685, horses feeding in the meadows of North America, near the bay of St Louis, which were so ferocious that nobody durst come near them. Oexmelin fays, that he has seen large troops of them in St Domingo running in the valleys ; that when any per,- fon approached, they all ftopt ; and one of them would advance till within a certain distance, then snort with his nose, take to his heels, and the whole troop after him. Every author who takes notice of these horses of America, agree that they are smaller and lefshandfome than those of Europe. These relations sufficiently prove, that the horse , when at full liberty, though not a fierce or dangerous animal, has.no inclination to associate with mankind ; that all the softness and ductility of his temper proceeds entirely from the culture and polish he receives in his domestic education, which in some measure commences as soon as he is brought forth.

The motions of the horse are chiefly regulated by the bit and the spur; the bit informs him how to direct his course, and the spur quickens his pace. The mouth of the horse is endowed with in amazing sensibility : the ftighteft motion or pressure of the bit gives, him warning, and instantly determines his course

The horse has not only agrandeur in his general appearance, but there is the great eft symmetry and proportion in the different parts of his body. The regularity and proportion of the different parts of the head gives him an air of lightness, which is well sup ported by the strength and beauty of his chest. He ereCts his head, as if willing to exalt himself above the condition of other, quadrupeds : his eyes are open and lively;

But the foals produced by such early embraces are generally ill made and weakly. Mares go with young eleven months and some days. They bring forth (landing ; contrary to the course of most other quadrupeds, who lie during. this operation. They continue to bring forth till the age of 16 or 18 years ; and both horses and mares live between .25 and 30 years. Horses cast their hair once a year, general ly in the spring, but sometimes in the autumn. At this time they are weak, and require to be better fed and taken care of than at any other season.

In Persia, Arabia, and most eastern countries, they never geld their horses, as is done in Europe and China. This operation greatly diminishes their strength, courage, and spirit; but it mukes them good humoured, gentle, and traiftable. With regard to the time of performing this operation, the practice of different

countries is different: some geld their horses when ayear old, and others at 18 months. But the best and most general practice is to delay the operation till they be two years old at least; because, when the gelding is delayed for two years or more, the animals retain more of the strength and other qualities which naturally belong to the male.

As the utility of horses surpasses that of all other domestic animals, it may be of use to subjoin some marks by which the age and other properties of horses may be distinguished.

The first teeth that appear are four, two above and two below, which are called foal-teeth, and may be easily distinguished from the others by their whiteness. The reft come out afterwards till they are twelve in number, six above and six below. When a colt is between two years and a half and three years old, he casts four of these teeth, two above and two below. These we call nippers or gatherers, and are much longer and larger than the fore teeth ; with these he nips off the grafs, and pulls the hay from the rack. When these are complete, the "horse will be three years old, or somewhat more.

When he is about four, he casts again two above and two below, one on each side the nippers; so that now there are no fore teeth remaining but the corner teeth ; and hence it may be concluded that he is about four years old. The tusks appear next after these,. and are a little crooked Those below come out before those on the upper jaw. and at four years old they are very small . When all the colt -teeth are cast, and the corner-teeth begin to (hew themselves, then the horse comes five.

From five to five apd a half the corner teeth" remain; hollow within, and are not quite filled up till the horse is six. At five and a half they are about a quarter of an inch high, and when he is full six near half an inch. Everything that is to be examined at six years old, are the corner-teeth and the tusks That part of the corner-teeth that had flesh in it first turns to a brownish spot, . like the eye of a gard fin-bean. At seven the mark or spot becomes feint, and the tooth more even. At eight it quite disappears though it possibly may remain in a very small degree for two^r three years more, which has deceived many, Themjiger the corner teeth are, “the older is the horse ; and ftiey are apt to grow soul and turn yellow. When the mark is gone, if you touch the tusks on the upper jaw with your finger, arid find it worn away and equal with the palate, you may certainly judge that the horse is ten years old at least. Laftly, when the flanks of a horse are much funk, the. feet broken and -spoiled, the pace : bad, and the eye-pits very yellow, you may certainly conclude the horse is considerably advanced in years.

The finews and the bones should be so diftinff, as to make the legs appear thin and lathy, not full and round. The pattern joints fhopldnever be large and round;;

With regard to the colour of a horse, the bright bay, and indeed all kinds of bays in general, are accounted a good colour. The chesnut horse is generally preferable to the sorrel, unless the former happens to be bald, or party-coloured with white legs. Brown horses have generally black manes and tails, and their joints are of a rusty black. Those of this colour that are dappled are much hands omer than the reft. Horses of a shining black, and well-marked, without too much white, are in high esteem for their beauty. A star, or blaze, or white muzzle, or one or more feet tipped with white, are thought to be rather better than those that are quite black.

Of greys, the dappled are accounted best ; though the silver grey makes a more beautiful appearance, aBd often prove good. The iron grey with white manes and tails are thought not to be so hardy. Greys of every kind will turn white sooner or later; but the nutmeg grey, when the dappled parts incline to bay or chesnut, are said to bs good hardy horses. Roan horses have a diversity of colours mixed together ; but the white is more predominant than the reft. They are all generally hardy, and fit for the road ; and some are exceeding good. Those of a strawberry colour mod resemble the sorrel', and they are often marked with white on the face and legs. When the bay is blended with it, he seems to be tinctured with claret ; and some of these prove to be very good. Dun, fallow, and cream-coloured horses have a lift down their backs ; and their manes and tales are black.

Those horses that are finely spotted with gay colours like leopards are a great rarity, and for that reason are only in the hands of great men.

There is some difference in horses according to the different countries where they are bred. For instance, in France, those of Bretagne are pretty strong made, and have generally black hair, or brown bay ; and they have good legs and feet, with a hardy mouth, and a head short and fleshy ; but in general they are pretty clumsy. The horses of Franche Compte are said to have the legs of tigers, and the belly of a hind ; but they are Ihort and thick, and of a middle size ; being much more proper for drawing than riding.

The horses of Gascony are not unlike those of Spain ; but they are not so handsome, nor so aftive, and therefore they are more proper to draw carriages. The Limofin horses are very vicious, and are good for little till they are six years old. Their colour is generally bay, or a bay brown. The horses of Normandy are much like those of Bretagne ; and those of Poitou have good bodies, legs, feet, and eyes ; but they are far from being handsome.

The horses of Germany are much better and more handsome than those of the Low countries. They are of great use for carriages ; but much more for the army, and for drawing the artillery. They have a great deal of hair, especially about the legs. They are not large, but they are web set ; and yet they have tender feet. The Hungarian horses are excellent for the coach, as well 4s for riding ; but they are large, though well proportioned, and they are of all colours, and in general very fwiftv

The British horses are of all kinds, they having been brought at first from different countries ; but for racers no country can equal them, they having been b*red from 'what are called barbs. The Danish horses are low, Ihort, and square; but they have a fine head, and sliort hair. The horses of the Low countries are very fit for the coach, and they are bell known by the name of Flanders-mares. The Polish horses are like the Danish; only they have not so fine a fore-hand: their colour is generally a bright bay, and that of the outward peel of an onion ; and they are fiery and vicious. The horses of Switzerland are pretty much like those of Germany ; which is bo wonder, since the Germans purchase a great number of them. The horses of Piedmont are fiery, of a middle size, and of all forts of colours ; their legs are good and handsome, their eyes fine, their ears small, and their mouths good ; but they do not carry their heads well.

The horses of Naples and Italy are generally ill made, and lean ; and yet they are good and useful, for they are light and proper for racing, though not for a long course ; they never do well in a colder climate.

The Spanish horses are very well made, and handsome, as well as very ad five and nimble ; they have good eyes, handsome legs and heads, and are easily managed : Vol. II. No. 47.

The a Is is likewise a domestic animal, and easily distinguished from the horse at first fight ; we never confound these two animals, even though they Ihould happen to be of the same colour and stature ; however, when we view the different parts of the ass, whether the external or internal, and compare them with the corresponding parts of the horse, the resemblance of these parts is so per fest, that we are surprised to find the individuals so different and so easily distinguishable by the eye From this circumftanGe, some naturalists have confidered the ass and the horse to be the same species of animals ; and that the small differences between them are accidental, or owing to the influence of climate, culture, &c. Linnaeus’s specific mark of the horse is, that the whole tail is covered with long hair ; and his specific mark of the ass is, that the tail has long hair only towards the point, and a black cross over the (shoulders. On the other hand, when we consider the differences in the temper, the manners and dispositions of these two animals, and, above all, the 2 5 M impoifiE CL u (5

impossibility of mining them so as to produce a common or intermediate species capable of propagating .and transmitting in the same manner as other diftiniff species, the notion that the horse and the ass are the same species will appear to be without any solid foundation. Besides, the ass differs materially from the horse in the thickness of the head, the length of the ears, the hardness of the (kin, and in the voice, the dispositions, the manner of drinking, 6c. With regard to animals, there is perhaps but one permanent and uniform specific diftimflion in nature : a male and female of different species may copulate, may produce a third animal resembling both, but very different from either: but here nature has put a final flop to all further procreation: the third animal, although it be feemingl y furnished with every thing necessary for propagating, remains for ever barren. Now, the horse may be made to copulate with the ass ; a mule, or mixture of the two, is the fruit of the unnatural embrace : but the impregnation of a mule is found by experience to be altogether impossible.

The ass, therefore, is a distinct species, and his race as ancient as that of the horse. Why then (should this useful, patient, fober animal be so much despised? We are apt to compare him, on every occasion, with the horse, and from this comparison are led to very false and. unfavourable conclusions. The horse is educated with great care and expence ; while the poor ass* abandoned to the abuse of the meanest servants or the cruelty of Children, instead of deriving benefit’ from inftrudlion, loses in effect his natural good qualities by the bad treatment he fuffers. He is the sport and buffet-block of every ruftic, who beat and overload him without mercy or discretion. They never confider, that the ass would be the most useful, the belt made, and moll dirtinguiftied of all animals, if there were no horses in the world.

The ass is as humble, patient, and tranquil, as the horse is bold, ardent, and impetuous. He submits with firmness, perhaps with magnanimity, to strokes and Chastisement ; he is temperate both as to the quantity and quality of his food ; he contents himself with the rigid and disagreeable herbage which the horse and other animals leave to him, and disdain to eat : he i3 more delicate with regard to his drink, never using water, unless it be persedly" pure. As his mailer does not take the trouble of combing him, he often rolls himself on the turf among thirties, ferns, 6c. Without regarding what he is carrying, he lies down to roll as often as he can, seeming to reproach his mailer for neglect and want of attention.

When very young, the ass is a gay, sprightly, nimble, and gentle animal. But he soon loses these qualities, probably by the bad usage he meets with ; and becomes lazy, umradtable, and stubborn. When under the influence of love, he becomes perfectly furious. The asse&ion of the female for her young is strong : Pliny assures us, that when an experiment was made to discover the strength of maternal asse&ion in a Ihe-ass, file run through the flames in order to come at her colt;

The Dutch have been at great pains to tame and use them for domestic purposes, but with little \ success. He is hard-mouthed, and kicks when any person attempts to touch or come near him. erinaceus.c:

There are three species, viz. i. The europseus, or. common hedge-hog, with round ears, and crested noftrila. It is about nine inches long; the upper part of the body is totally covered with fliarp prickles, and the under part is covered with hair. The hedge-hog,, even when Handing on his legs, has a very ugly afpedf. His body is an oblong mafs, convex above, terminated on the fore-part by a very ffiarp muzzle, and mount.ed on four fi ort legs, of which nothing appears but the feet, and the tail is not discernible. His ears are broad, round, and fi ort ; and his eyes are small and protuberant. The length of his body, from the point of the muzzle to the anus, is about nine indies.

The hedge-hog has a very uncommon method of defending himself from the attacks of other animals : being possessed of little strength or agility, he does not attempt to fly from or assail his enemies ; but erects his biiftlts, and rolls himself up like a ball, expofmg no*

part:

^part of his body that is not furnished with sharp, weapons of defence ; he will not unfold himself, unless thrown into water: the more he is frightened or havra/Ted, the clot ler he (huts himself up, and frequently discharges his urine, which has a very foe tid an lothsome finest. While in this state, most dogs, instead of biting him, (land off and bark, not daring to seize him ; or, if they attempt it once, their mouths are so pricked with his bristles, that they cannot be prevailed on to attempt it a second time. Both the male and female are covered with bristles from the head to the tail. These bristles are of great use in defending them from other animals ; but must be very inconvenient when they incline to copulate. This operation they cannot perform in the manner of other quadrupeds ; but do it face to face, either Handing on end, or the female dying on her back. The females come • in season in the spring, and bring forth their young in the beginning of summer. They commonly bring forth three or four, and sometimes five, at a time. The young ones are qf a whitish colour, and only the points of the bristles appear above the llcin. It is impossible to tame them : the mother and her young have frequently been confined together, and furnished with plenty of provisions : but, instead of nourishing them, fhe uniformly devoured them one after another. Males and females have likewise been kept in one apartment, where they lived, but never copulated. Hedge-hogs feed upon fallen fruits some roots, and infe&s : they are very fond of flesh-meat, whether raw or roasted. They frequent woods, and live under the trunks of old trees, inthe chinks of rocks, or under large stones. Naturalists alledge that they go into gardens, mount the trees, and come down with pears, apples, or plumbs, stuck upon their bristles. But this is a mistake: although kept in a garden, they never attempt to climb trees, or flick even fallen fruit upon their •bristles, but, lay hold of their food with their mouth. They never come out of their holes in theday, but go about in quest of food during the night. They eat but little, and can live very long without taking any nourishment. They do not lay up any store of provisions in harvest ; such an inst int would be useless, as they sleep all the winter. See Plate LXXIV fig. 6.

etching.c:
ETCHING, a method of engraving on copper, in which the lines or strokes, indeed of being cut with a tool or graver, are eaten in with aquafortis.

Etching is done with more ease and expedition than engraving : it requires fewer indruments, and represents molt kind of fubjeefs better and more agreeable to nature, as landscapes, ruins, grounds, and all small, faint, loose, remote objeCis, buildings, <bc. See Engraving.

The method of etching is as follows : Chuse the copperplate as dire died for engraving, and furnish yourself with a piece of ground, tied up in a bit of thin silk, kes>t very clean, to be laid upon the plate, when both have been warmed; proper needles, to hatch with on the ground ; a pencil or br unfit, to wipe away the bits of ground which rife afterits hatching ; a polisher ; two or three gravers ; a pa;r of compasses. to measure didances and draw circles ; a ruler, to hatch straight lines; green wax, to make the. wall round the edges of the plate, to contain the aquafortis ; an oil-done; a bottle of aquafortis; some red lead, to colour the back side of the copy ; a dist, and a hand-vice, to hold the plate over the candle. See Needle, Graver, Polisher, Compass, fee.

To make the ground, take three ounces -of asphaltum, two ounces of clean rosin,ha!f an ounce of Bur- .gnndy-pitch, three ounces of black wax, and three

ounces of vSrg'n-wax*. let ail these be melted in a clean earthern pipkin over a flow fire, stirring it all the time with a fniall dick ; if it burn »o the bottom, it is spoiled. After the ingredients are well melted, and it boils up, put it intoa pan of fair water; and before it l:e quite cold, take it out, and roll it into small lumps to be kept from dud : this ground is what others call the varnifli. The next thing s to clean the plate to receive the ground : take a piece of lifting, roll it up as big as an egg, tie it very tight, so as to make it a rubber; and having dropped a small quantity of sweet oil, and added a little powder of rotten done on the plate, rub it with this ball, till it will almost shew your face. Then wipe it all off with a dean rag ; and after that, make it quite dry with another clean rag and a little fine whitening:

The next thing is to lay on the varnifli ; to do which aright you mud take a handvice, and six it at the middle cf one part of the plate, with a piece of paper between the teeth of the hand-vice and the plate, to prevent the marks of the teeth : then laying the plate on a chafHng-dHh, with a small charcoal fire in it, tirl the plate be so hot, that, by spitting on the back-side* the wet will fly off: rub the plate with the ground tied Up in silk, till it be covered all over ; and after that daub the plate with a piece of cotton wrapped up in silk, till the ground be quite smooth, keeping the plate a little warm all the time. The varnifli being thus smoothed upon the plate, it mud be blacked in-the following manner: take a thick tallow candle that burns clear, with a short snuff ; and having driven two nails into the waM, to let it red upon, place the plate against the wall with the varnish side downward, and take care not to touch the ground with your fingers : then taking the candle, apply the flame to the varnifli as close as possible, without touching the varnifli with the snuff of the candle, and guide the flame all over it, till it become perfectly black. After this is done, and the plate dry, the design is traced with ance dle through the varnifli, and a rim or border of wax is raised round the circumference of the plate; and then the artist has a composition of common varnifli and lamp-black, made very thin, wherewith he covers the parts that are not to be bitten, by means of a hair-pencil. And he is every now and then covering or uncovering this or that part of the design, as occasion may require • the conduct of the aquafortis being the principal concern, on which the effect of the print very much depends The operator mut be attentive to the ground, that it does r.ot fail in any part,, and where it does to flop up the place with the above composition Theplate is defended from the aquafortis every where, but in the lines or hatches cut through it withthe needle, through which the water eats into the copper to the depth required ; remembering to keep it stirring with a feather all the while; which done, it is to be poured off again.

Single aquafortis is most commonly used ; and if it betoo strong, mix it with vinegar, otherwise it will make the work very hard, and sometimes break, up the ground : tbe aquafortis .having done its part, the ground

And, laftly, it is to be remembered, that a fresh dip of aquafortis is never given, without first washing out the plate in fair water, and drying it at the fire.

"ETERNITY, an attribute of God, expressing his infinite or endless duration.

ETHIOPIA, or ^Ethiopia, a very extensive country of Africa, comprehending Abyssinia, Nubia, and Abex : it is bounded by Egypt, and the desert of Barca, on the north ; by the Red sea and Indian ocean, on the east ; by Anian, and the unknown parts of Africa, on the south ; and by other unknown countries on the weft.

etna.c: ETNA, or mount Gibello, a vulcano, or burning mountain of ,Sicily, situated fifty miles south-weft of Meflina, and twenty weft of Catania. See Vulcano.

etymology.c: ETYMOLOGY, that part of grammar which confiders and explains the origin and derivation of words, in order to arrive at their first and primary signification. See Gjrammar.

evacuants.c: EVACUANTS, in pharmacy, are properly such medicines as diminish the animal fluids, by throwing out some morbid or redundant humour, or such as thin, attenuate, and promote the motion and circulation thereof.

evacuation.c: EVACUATION, in medicine, the art of diminishing, emptying, or attenuating the humours of the body. See Medicine.

evangelist.c:
EVANGELIST, a general name given to those who write or preach the gospel of Jesus Christ.

The word is of Greek origin, signifying one who publishes glad tiding, or is the messenger of good news.

According to Hooker, evangelists were presbyters of principal sufficiency, whom die apostles sent abroad, and used as agents in ecclesiastical affairs, wheresoever they saw need.

The term evangelist however is at present confined to the writers of the four gospels.

-EVANID, a name given by some authors to such colours as are of no long duration, as those in the rainbow, in clouds before and after sun-set, fee.

Evanid colours are also called fantastical and emphatical colours.

rEV ANTES, in antiquity, the priestesses of Bacchus, thus called, by reason, that in celebrating the orgia, they ran about as if distracted, crying, Evan, evan, one evan. See Bacchanalia.

^EVAPORATION, in chemistry, the fetting a liquor in a.,.gemle heat jo discharge its superfluous humidity, reduce it to a proper consistence, or obtain its dry remainder. See ClfEMlSTR Y.

evates.c: EVATES, a branch or division of the druids, or ancient Celtic philosophers. Strabo divides the British and Gaulish philosophe is into three se«5Vs ; bards, evates, and druids. He adds, that the bards were the poets and musicians ; the evates, the priests and naturalists • and the druids were moralists as well as naturalists: But Marcellus and Hornius reduce them all to two sects, viz. the bards and druids.

eubages.c: EUBAGES, an order of priests, or philosophers, among the ancient Celt®, or Gauls : some will have the cub ages to be the same with the druids and faronidae of DiodoTus; and others, that they were the same with what Strabo calls evates.

eucharist.c:
EUCHARIST, the sacrament of the Lord’s supper, prop oily signifies giving thanks.

This sacrament was instituted by Christ himself, and the participation of it called communion.

As to the manner of celebrating the eucharist among the ancient Christians, after the customary oblations were/made, the deacon brought water to the bishops and presbyters, (landing round the table, to waft their hands, according to that of the psalmist, “ I will wa.Tt my hands in innocency, and so will I “ compass thy altar, O Lord.” Then the deacon cried out aloud, “ Mutually embrace and kifs each “ other;” which being done, the whole congregation prayed for the universal peace and welfare of the church, for the tranquillity and repose of the world, for the prosperity of the age, for wholesome weather, and for all ranks and degrees of men. After this followed mutual salutations of the minister and people ; and then the bishop or presbyter having fantftified the elements by a solemn benediction, he brake the bread, and delivered it to the deacon, who distributed it to the communicants; and after that the cup. Their sacramental wine was usually diluted or mixed with water. During the time of administration, they fang hymns and psalms ; and, having concluded with prayer and thanksgiving, the people saluted each other with a kifs of peace, and so the a flan b*y broke up.

They were a branch of Arians, and took their name from Eunomius, bishop of Cyzicus, who was instructed by iEtius, in the points which were then controverted in the church, after having at ■first followed the profession of arms. Eunomius so. well answered the designs of his master, and declaimed so vehemently against the divinity of the Word, that the people had recourse to the authority of the prince, and had him banished; but the Arians obtained his recall, and elected him bishop of Cyzicus. EUROPE, the lead of the four grand divisions of the earth, is situated between 36° and 720 N. lat.; and between io° degrees W. long, and 6j° E. long, being about 3000 miles long from north to south, and 2500 miles broad from east to weft. It is bounded by the frozen ocean on the north, by Asia on the east, by the Mediterranean, which separates it from Africa, on the south, and by the Atlantic ocean on the weft.

Europe is commonly subdivided into three grand divisions, north, middle, and south. The north or upper division comprehends Russia, or Muscovy, Sweden, Denmark, and Norway, ar>d the islands of Biitain, Iceland. Greenland, and those of the Baltic. The middle division contains Poland, Germany, and the hereditary dominions of the house of Austria, the Low Countries, or Netheilands, and France.
